title: The P-38 Solved an Annoying Problem
text: The P-38 solved one of the most annoying engineering challenges of World War II, thanks to its unique engine configuration. It solved gun convergence. The central fuselage was like a ball turret, with wings and engines attached to it. It had four 50-caliber machine guns and a 20mm cannon, all pointing forward with zero convergence issues. Convergence issues plagued fighter planes of this era. With guns mounted directly in front of the target, lead their shots according to distance and speed, and pull the trigger. However, most World War II fighters had machine guns or cannons mounted in the wings, where they had more space to fit them. This raises the question, where should the guns actually point? You could point them forward and have two hit zones coming from each wing, but this spread of bullets would make aiming a nightmare and almost guarantee multiple misses in a single burst, even with perfect aim. Or you can angle them in slightly, so that they converged at an optimum distance in front of the pilot. But now the question was, what was the optimum distance? This distance would determine how close the pilot had to be in a dogfight. For fast turning, close quarter, fighter on fighter action, you wanted a shortened convergence point. text: Some guns are accurate at long range. Some guns are compact and easy to carry. Some guns make it easy to have a drink. After the Six-Day War in 1967, the Israeli Defense Force or IDF needed a replacement for the FAL, whose performance was underwhelming. After studying captured AKs, the end result was the Gileo. As an aside, the Gileo was based on the AK-47, invented by Mikhail Kailashnikov. By a bit of historical irony, Gileo's inventor was Yizarel Balashnikov. Anyway, the Gileo was chambered in 5.56mm and it came in three variants, the standard automatic rifle machine gun, an automatic rifle, and a short automatic rifle, though other variants would follow in the later years. It was designed to be as ergonomic as possible, with the charging handle protruding from the upper receiver, so left or right-handed shooters can use it with equal efficiency, and also had a folding carry handle. One of the more noteworthy features, however, has nothing to do with the function of the firearm. IDF troops had a bad habit of using the front lip of magazines as bottle openers, which would damage the thin metal. To prevent equipment damage, the Gileo came equipped with a built-in bottle opener. Located at the base of the foregrip, it's, well, a bottle opener. This isn't a part that can be improvised as a bottle opener, but a dedicated purpose-built new feature that was added in purely for a soldier's benefit, and to protect the equipment from damage due to improper use.
